text:
I found Q3.5 sensitive data confusing because we had two different thresholds: one for identification gain and another purely for fairness. It felt artificial to separate them; usually, trade-offs go together. I struggled with that distinction as well.

This was most important for me regarding the model design. If we can prove the system works equally well without using sensitive data first, then it shouldn't be used at all—that's an outside-the-model solution. On fairness versus accuracy: I voted "never" on collecting race/ethnicity or nationality even if it improves identification because my experience as a Faroese student shows that small differences in treatment can lead to severe stigma and alienation. Collecting these traits risks causing more harm than good, so they should remain optional only for those who explicitly want support based on specific contexts rather than broad profiling.

I found Q3 and Q4 especially tricky when balancing privacy against utility. As an advisor with 11 years of experience, I see students who feel targeted rather than supported if we can't explain *why* they're flagged clearly enough (Q4). The group largely agrees high sensitivity data is risky; my vote for 'never' on race/ethnicity reflects a fear that even small accuracy gains are overshadowed by the stigma it creates. We could resolve this tension not in the model itself, but by mandating an opt-out mechanism where students can choose to share sensitive context only when they believe it's necessary for tailored help—putting agency back with them rather than relying on broad data collection to drive outreach.

I struggled with Q3.5 because I am female and international but did not experience discrimination or health issues during my studies; thus, it was hard to separate identification concerns from fairness worries for myself (Q3 vs Q6). However, I agree that collecting nationality is risky due to potential stigma among peers who feel surveilled. For data related to my own context—like being a first-gen student—it would be acceptable with only a small improvement because identifying me early prevents falling behind before leaving the system as happened in previous studies. The most critical tension remains whether we can build fairness into existing data sources like course credits and performance grades rather than adding new sensitive categories entirely, which seems to require an opt-out mechanism for true privacy respect.

I found Q3.4 (Absalon data) particularly hard because page views feel like invasive surveillance compared to grades or credits I already have access to for my own planning. While some argued it's necessary to catch struggling students early, others rightly pointed out that tracking digital behavior crosses a line into constant monitoring. This tension highlights why explainability is crucial—if we use such data without clear context for the student, trust evaporates immediately. My view differs slightly on financial aid; I accepted using this with only a moderate improvement because funding barriers are tangible and actionable, unlike racial or national identity markers that create stigma rather than solving study issues. The real solution likely lies in letting students voluntarily share sensitive contexts when they seek tailored help, rather than forcing broad profiling to drive outreach proactively.

I struggled with Q3.4 because Absalon activity feels like surveillance compared to grades I can already see myself. However, on financial aid data (Q3.5), I supported using it if identification improves moderately; funding barriers are tangible and actionable for me as a working student, unlike race or nationality which cause stigma. My view differed from some regarding Q4 explainability: I voted "never" for low explainability because without clear reasons like credits failed, the flag feels punitive rather than helpful to students trying in progress. This tension suggests we need opt-out mechanisms where sensitive data is shared voluntarily by those who want tailored help, restoring agency and trust beyond just model design adjustments.

I found Q4.1 very low explainability hard to answer; trusting a black box contradicts my role helping students understand their struggles. The biggest tension is between "catching" all struggling learners and respecting privacy for sensitive data like nationality or disability status, which often triggers stigma rather than support. I answered that only significant identification gains justify using this data, but some peers were more cautious due to fairness risks. If the group agrees on a strict opt-out mechanism where students voluntarily share specific context for tailored help instead of broad profiling, it might resolve these trade-offs without needing complex models at all. My main concern is ensuring trust outweighs utility unless we have clear agency back with individuals.

I found Q3.4 particularly challenging; tracking page views feels like invasive surveillance compared to grades I control myself for my own planning, creating an immediate trust barrier. Regarding fairness (Q3.6), while age helps contextualize my chronic health condition with a small improvement threshold, collecting race/ethnicity or nationality is risky due to potential stigma rather than actionable support.

The key tension lies between "catching" everyone efficiently and respecting privacy through agency. Many agreed that opt-out mechanisms for voluntary data sharing could resolve these trade-offs without relying on broad profiling models at all. This approach puts control back in students' hands, ensuring the system supports us early while avoiding unnecessary monitoring or stigma unless we explicitly choose to share sensitive context for tailored help.

I found Q3.6 hardest because it felt artificial to accept using nationality data *only* if it improved fairness, knowing that small biases against my group are already baked into current systems. My 'acceptable regardless' vote for first-gen and financial aid was driven by tangible barriers I face; these help me directly without the stigma of racial profiling. The biggest tension is between catching struggling students early versus protecting privacy from surveillance. While some prefer broad data collection, others rightly fear it creates distrust or alienation. I agree that an opt-out mechanism might resolve this better than redesigning the model: let us voluntarily share specific context when we want tailored help, rather than forcing our entire academic history into a black box for proactive outreach.

I found Q3.5's separation of identification vs fairness thresholds artificial; usually they go together. Regarding my answers: I accepted disability and financial aid data only if it offered tangible, small-to-moderate improvements for me personally. However, I rejected age/gender/nationality/race entirely to avoid stigma, which created a tension with the "catching everyone" goal because missing some struggling peers could be worse than profiling others. This highlights that even good models aren't enough; we need an opt-out mechanism where students voluntarily share sensitive context for tailored help instead of broad proactive surveillance.

I found Q3.6 tricky because I often assume data like nationality or race would cause harm rather than help identify me specifically—I'm Danish after all, so that distinction feels abstract without context for my disability support needs. My biggest tension was balancing catching struggling peers with avoiding surveillance stigma; many agreed that broad profiling erodes trust unless we have explicit consent. The real solution lies outside the model: an opt-out mechanism where students voluntarily share specific contexts only when they believe it's necessary for tailored help, rather than relying on passive data collection to drive outreach proactively. I think agency must outweigh utility here.

I struggled with Q3.6 because my answers felt contradictory: I accepted disability data only if it improved fairness due to stigma risks, but found gender and nationality acceptable regardless for broader inclusion. The core tension is balancing early catch-up against surveillance fears. Many others correctly identified that broad profiling erodes trust unless students have agency.

I agree completely with the solution proposed by S1-S5: we need an opt-out mechanism where I can voluntarily share sensitive context only if it genuinely helps tailored support, rather than forcing proactive outreach on everyone based on complex models. True acceptance requires moving beyond model design to restoring student control over their data and preventing unwanted stigma.

I found Q3.6 tricky because accepting "acceptable regardless" for first-gen students felt contradictory given my history of dropping out; I wanted safety nets but feared broad categorization. On fairness (Q5), I accepted a 3-student loss to ensure marginalized groups aren't missed, as excluding them perpetuates inequality. The group's focus on opt-out mechanisms resonates deeply: it shifts power from the institution predicting our struggles to us choosing when we seek help. However, I worry that without early identification tools like course performance data (Q3.2), these voluntary shares happen too late—after credits have been wasted. True support requires balancing proactive detection with agency; perhaps models should flag risks based on non-sensitive academic patterns first, inviting students to voluntarily share deeper context if needed later.
